messages.author: 93e2d4587d90a376
messages.subject: Occupancy model for nomadic species
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am interested in understanding the occupancy patterns of a nomadic species that move throughout the landscape, presumably given seasonal food availability. To capture these patterns, we are collecting monthly presence/absence data across all known roosting sites. The end goal is to understand the seasonal probability of occupancy across the region and investigate how different factors might explain some of these dynamics. This will hopefully provide a clearer picture of how these species use the landscape, which will be important for effective management.

I was wondering what the best approach to analysing this type of data would be if the species were intermittently present in an area. It would be important to understand whether the species was truly absent in an area or just went undetected at that particular time, so my default option was using some sort of dynamics occupancy model. However, this is the first time I have worked in a system like this, so I was hoping someone with more experience could point me in the right direction.

Thank you for your time.

All my best,

Alejandro

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Occupancy model for nomadic species
parts:
Hi Alejandro,

Traditional dynamic occupancy models require repeat sampling within periods of assumed closure. Say, every month you did a few surveys that were close together in time to estimate the occupancy for that particular month. In the absence of repeat surveys, say you just do one survey per month to inform the occupancy of that month, the model is not or weakly identified. If, on the other hand, you have something like automated recording units (ARUs) like SongMeters, then it becomes a lot easier to look at fine-grained site usage such as seasonal occupancy. What sort of data are you working with? That will help us to inform on a good model.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.author: 93e2d4587d90a376
messages.subject: Re: Occupancy model for nomadic species
parts:
Hi Matt,

Thanks for your quick response. I am thinking of how I will analyse the data before collecting it, so understanding the model requirements at this point is very useful because we can adapt our design accordingly.

Would dynamic occupancy models be able to capture the probability that the species has left, returned, or continuously stayed at each location for each month during the study period?

Assuming that dynamic occupancy models are the best tool to understand these nomadic dynamics, would you recommend we incorporate a more robust design with, say, three visits within a week (when we assume closure) and repeat this every month (when we assume that the species might or might not have left the location)? Here, I am assuming that closure means that the species occupies that site during the week we are repeating the survey and, therefore, absence is failing to be detected. These species live in large groups, so population closure in terms of number of individuals is uncertain (we are unsure if all individuals return to the same roost after foraging).

Thanks again for your time. I truly appreciate it.

All my best,

Alejandro

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Occupancy model for nomadic species
parts: Would dynamic occupancy models be able to capture the probability that the species has left, returned, or continuously stayed at each location for each month during the study period?

Short answer, yes. For each primary occasion (month in this case) you can get a posterior distribution for that site's occupancy state. If you're using maximum likelihood or the latent states are marginalised out in a Bayesian framework, you can still recover these. So yes, you will be able to make probabilistic claims about when sites were occupied.

Assuming that dynamic occupancy models are the best tool to understand these nomadic dynamics, would you recommend we incorporate a more robust design with, say, three visits within a week (when we assume closure) and repeat this every month (when we assume that the species might or might not have left the location)?

Yes. But if detection probability is really high, as in you'll basically certainly detect the species if it's present, then this is unnecessary. In this case, you can just use the results of single surveys as an indicator for occupancy.
These species live in large groups, so population closure in terms of number of individuals is uncertain (we are unsure if all individuals return to the same roost after foraging).

Yeah, closure here just refers to the occupancy state, so that the occupancy state doesn't change between your secondary surveys. If you were also interested in modeling latent abundance, something like an N-mixture model might work as well. But again, if detection probabilities are quite high, you might not even have to account for imperfect detection.

Cheers,

Matt
